sentences.text: Kumimanu is recognized as one of the largest penguin species ever discovered.
Specimens of Kumimanu biceae reached a total length of 177 cm and weighed approximately 101 kg.
Its size is surpassed only by the penguin genus Palaeeudyptes.
This ancient bird is older than any other previously discovered giant-sized penguin remains.
Measurements indicate the bird stood approximately 1.60 to 1.77 meters tall and weighed over 91 kg.
The genus name Kumimanu translates to monster bird in the Māori language.
The species name biceae honors Beatrice A. Tennyson, the mother of author Alan J. D. Tennyson.
Due to its large size, the animal likely consumed larger prey than modern penguins.
Fossils of Kumimanu were found in New Zealand and the discovery was announced in December 2017.
Researchers found Kumimanu fossils at Hampden Beach on the South Island of New Zealand.
The Kumimanu fossils originate from the Paleocene Waipara Greensand formation.
A New Zealand and German team led by Gerald Mayr studied the Kumimanu fossils.
The proposed species Kumimanu fordycei was named after a large specimen found by Alan Tennyson in 2017 from the late Palaeocene Moeraki Formation.

In 2025, Mayr et al. revised their findings to suggest that features distinguishing K. fordycei from K. biceae fall within the variation of a single species, identifying K. fordycei as a junior synonym of K. biceae.
Researchers suggest that K. biceae likely lived in a manner similar to modern penguins.
Kumimanu biceae is the type species of the genus Kumimanu.
The genus Kumimanu includes the species K. biceae and the proposed species K. fordycei.
Kumimanu is classified within the family Spheniscidae.
Kumimanu lived approximately 56 to 60 million years ago during the Paleocene epoch.
Kumimanu biceae lived in New Zealand, which was subtropical for much of the Paleocene.
The time range for Kumimanu is estimated from 59.24 to 56 million years ago.
